characters: Eyram: a fourteen-year-old Ghanaian JHS 3 prefect in a reflective road-warden sash over her uniform.
Kojo: her classmate holding a spring balance, wooden block, and ruler for physics tests.
Abdulai: their classmate whose uncle drives a commercial trotro minibus responsibly.
Corporal Adjei: a Ghana Police Motor Traffic and Transport Department (MTTD) officer in crisp uniform.

narrationPlan.voice: Alert teen voices for Eyram, Kojo, and Abdulai; steady, authoritative voice for MTTD Corporal Adjei
narrationPlan.pace: Crisp, urgent, and analytical (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with distinct, natural voices for each JHS student, teacher, and community specialist.
Pause for two seconds at each comprehension check so learners can reason before answering.
Never rush the final page: let the scientific and moral synthesis settle clearly.

music: Steady rhythmic percussion with rain ambience resolving into calm, confident acoustic chords (placeholder)
culturalNotes: NaCCA CCP Alignment: Integrated Science (B8.4.4.1 / B9.4.4.1: Strand 4, Sub-strand 4: Force and Motion—friction, momentum, pressure P = F/A, centre of gravity and stability), Social Studies (B8.4.1.1 / B9.4.1.1: Strand 4: Law and Order—road safety regulations and causes of crashes), and RME (B7.5.1.1 / B8.5.1.1: Sanctity of human life, patience, and civic responsibility).

Ghana Traffic Convention: Ghana drives on the RIGHT-hand side (since 1974), so traffic in the nearest lane approaches from the LEFT. Learners look left, right, and left again, and must wait on the kerb until vehicles reach a complete standstill.

teacherGuide.overview: Uses a vivid rainy-day school-crossing near-miss to teach core BECE mechanics (friction, kinetic energy, pressure P = F/A, and centre of gravity/stability) alongside National Road Safety Authority rules and moral respect for human life.
learningGoals: Explain how road wetness, tyre tread depth, speed, and vehicle mass affect friction and braking distance.
Calculate pressure using P = F ÷ A and apply it to seatbelts, sharp tools, and tyres.
Explain how high roof-rack loading raises centre of gravity and reduces vehicle stability.
Connect civic traffic laws with religious and traditional moral duties to preserve human life.

beforeReading: Rub dry palms briskly together (feel heat from friction), then rub soapy wet palms—how does grip change?
whileReading: Pause on Page 3 to solve a quick board calculation comparing pressure from a narrow strap vs a wide seatbelt.
afterReading: Measure friction across dry desk wood, rough concrete, and wet plastic tray using a spring balance and weighted block.
discussion: Which road risks can drivers and passengers identify and prevent before a crash happens?
reflection: As a passenger, what polite, firm words can you use if a driver speeds or overtakes blindly on a hill?

mathsExtension.task: During sudden braking, a forward force of 1,200 N acts against a passenger’s seatbelt. Compare the pressure exerted by a proper wide seatbelt of contact area 0.06 m² versus a twisted thin strap of area 0.01 m².
mathsExtension.answer: Wide seatbelt: P = 1,200 N ÷ 0.06 m² = 20,000 Pa (20 kPa). Twisted thin strap: P = 1,200 N ÷ 0.01 m² = 120,000 Pa (120 kPa)—six times as much bruising pressure!

support: Use two matchboxes—one weighted at the bottom and one weighted on top—tilted slowly on a book to demonstrate centre of gravity.
stretch: Explain Pascal’s Principle in hydraulic braking systems and why air bubbles cause spongy brakes.

factCheck.claim: Water films reduce road-tyre friction, requiring grooved treads to evacuate water, while braking distance increases with vehicle mass and speed squared.
factCheck.explanation: Hydroplaning occurs when fluid pressure lifts the tyre off the road surface. Overloading raises kinetic energy (½mv²) and elevates centre of gravity, increasing overturning risk on curves.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA CCP Integrated Science B8.4.4.1 / B9.4.4.1 & National Road Safety Authority (NRSA) Ghana.
